On August [XXX], 2022 Toyota received a field report related to this crash. The vehicle was reportedly traveling east on [XXX], when it approached a vehicle travelling the wrong way on the road operated by a drunk driver. The Toyota Corolla driver alleged that they attempted to swerve right to miss the oncoming vehicle, but collided with the vehicle on the driver side. As a result of the collision, the Toyota Corolla allegedly rolled over, landed on its wheels, and contacted a highway barrier. 
Toyota obtained Vehicle Control History (VCH) and Event Data Recorder (EDR) data from the subject vehicle. VCH provides an approximately 8 second pre-crash data recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.80 second pre-crash data recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed:  Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged during the recording until approximately 6.7 seconds prior to the crash event and Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) was engaged during the recording until approximately 5.5 seconds prior to the crash event. ADAS L2 was disengaged approximately 6.7 seconds prior to the crash due to driver steering input exceeding the steering torque override threshold of LTA. The vehicle was traveling at approximately 89 MPH prior to the crash event. 
As a result of the crash incident, the subject vehicle was towed away from the scene. Injuries to occupants of the subject vehicle were described by the owner as: Driver: Cerebral fluid leaking from nose, Concussion, whiplash, backpain Front Passenger: No injuries reported.

During the call, she reported the vehicle hit some items on the side of the road, the wheels were bent, and the driver's door would not open properly. The customer reported that the vehicle was towed and that repairs are close to being completed.  In addition, she reported that although she was not injured, she went to the doctor and hospital for exacerbation of pre-existing conditions.
10/[XXX]/2022 Update: On October [XXX], 2022, Nissan inspected the vehicle at an independent repair facility, which is the location that the customer had the vehicle directly towed to after the incident. From pictures provided by the repair facility, Nissan identified possible damage to the center of the vehicle's left front wheel, a broken lower front control arm, a bent tie rod end, and the strut. No other incident-related body damage is visible in the photographs. The photos appear to show that the vehicle experienced a localized impact to the wheel, which generated force into in the location of the lower control arm.
During Nissan's in-person inspection of the vehicle, the vehicle repairs were near completion. In particular, the left front wheel was not available to Nissan at the time of inspection. Vehicle mileage at the time of inspection was 14,326. No data retrieval or ECU resets were performed by Nissan. As of this report, the vehicle has not been taken to a Nissan dealer.
Based on the photos reviewed and Nissan's inspection, the localized impact was insufficient to trigger an EDR recordable event. Therefore, Nissan is unable to determine customer inputs to the vehicle at the time of the incident. Separately, no event was recorded within the PPA system, indicating that PPA was not active at the time of the event.

The customer/driver of the subject vehicle notified Volkswagen Group of America (VWGoA) of an incident that occurred while traveling on the highway with travel assist (SAE L2 system) activated. According to the customer, they unexpectedly lost control of the vehicle in which it veered to the right, impacting the concrete wall / sound barrier.
Prior to impact, the customer stated they were driving in a marked construction zone, in the left lane, and it had recently began raining with the surface of the road noted as wet, but not pooling. To the left of the customer was a concrete median barrier, dividing the highway, and to the right was the right driving lane, then a narrow shoulder with construction barrels and the concrete wall / sound barrier.  
The frontal impact between the vehicle and the sound barrier resulted in the airbags deploying and then the vehicle coming to a rest in the right lane of the highway. There were no reported injuries, no additional road users involved, and police were notified and provided a report as well as a citation to the driver.  The vehicle was towed from the scene and is currently in possession of the insurance company. VWGoA plans to further investigate this matter and will submit subsequent reports accordingly.
Update Report 8/15/2024:  VWGoA conducted an inspection of the subject vehicle and information from the airbag control module (ACM) identified a speed of 70 to 68mph from -5.0 to -3.5 seconds precrash. After -3.0 seconds, the report reflects ABS and ESC activity all the way until 0.0 seconds suggesting a loss of control, possibly from the weather event reported by the customer or driver inputs. The front radar module was no longer with the vehicle at the time of the inspection and no EDR or ASM (Assist System Monitor) data was able to be obtained. The precise cause of the crash could not be determined, but no manufacturing shortcoming was identified.

Narrative: The May Mobility vehicle (Ego) is stopped at a red light, then the Ego begins to accelerate and turn right when the traffic light changes to green. As the Ego accelerates, a pedestrian begins moving and enters the crosswalk from the other side of the intersection. This activates the rule-based crosswalk logic. Ego determines that it is able to stop before the crosswalk without exceeding our max deceleration threshold, which triggers an in-policy stopping reaction for the crosswalk. The Ego brakes to yield for the pedestrian. The vehicle trailing the Ego accelerates, making contact with the rear-end of the Ego. In the 2.5 seconds between the start of the Ego braking and the collision, the rear vehicle accelerated from 0.2 to 6.1 m/s (0.4 to 13.6 mph) without slowing until after the collision occurred. In response to this incident, immediate mitigations were made, in that the vehicle operators (AVOs) operate all intersections in manual mode.  This remained in place until January 12, when we received a solution which instituted a reduction of the 3.5 m/s2 parameter, in order to prevent the Ego from yielding to pedestrians in crosswalks that are still far from the Egoâs lane if such yielding would induce braking.

On December [XXX], 2022, a Navya ARMA shuttle operated by Beep (VIN 1N9A1SACXJS[XXX]) was involved in a non-injury collision while operating in manual mode on [XXX] in Port Saint Lucie, FL.  While driving along [XXX] under autonomous control, the shuttle encountered a parked vehicle partially blocking its path, requiring disengagement of the autonomous drive system.  The safety driver attempted to manually drive the shuttle around the parked vehicle to reengage the autonomous drive system.  While manually steering the shuttle around the parked vehicle blocking its path, the shuttle failed to respond to manual control input and steered to the left, impacting a parked vehicle at a low rate of speed on the opposite side of [XXX].  The six passengers onboard alighted the shuttle, an accident report was filed with the local police, and the shuttle was removed from the scene.  Initial reports from the onboard safety driver indicated that while steering around the vehicle blocking the shuttle's path, the shuttle became unresponsive to control input.  The safety driver released the operator present button on the vehicle controller, which serves as dead man switch however, the vehicle failed to stop.  After the incident, further investigation by Navya confirmed that the root cause of the incident was a failure of the Xbox 360 controller used to manually control the vehicle.  Contact with the parked vehicle occurred between the time of failure and the vehicle drive system recognizing that the controller had failed an elapsed time of 4.05 seconds. In response to the incident, Beep suspended operation of all Navya ARMA vehicles pending identification and implementation of appropriate solutions to mitigate the risk of this failure leading to future incidents.
Subsequent investigation by Beep and Navya determined that the vehicle control software, NavyaDrive, is limited in its ability to monitor the validity of control signal input received from the Xbox 360 controller.  As the safety driver began to manually steer the vehicle, the controller failed, sending constant turning input to the vehicle drive system leading to the collision.  Though Navya developed software mitigations due to prior issues encountered with the controller, those mitigations were ineffective with respect to the failure leading to the incident on December [XXX].  Further, due to the short time between the controller failing and the collision (2.34sec), the safety driver was unable to identify the controller failure and trigger the emergency stop before the collision occurred.
In response to the incident, Navya is integrating a revised manual control system on the ARMA shuttle platform.  The revised manual control system utilizes industrial-grade components for improved electromechanical reliability and allows for active monitoring of the control system health, eliminating the root cause of the failure that led to the incident on December [XXX].  Software upgrades of all Navya ARMA vehicles will further reintroduce automated braking function while the ARMA vehicle is under manual control.  Beep is working with Navya to retrofit its fleet of ARMA vehicles with the revised manual control system as well as retrain and recertify its safety driver staff on the updated NavyaDrive software.
Discussion of the root cause analysis and solution design for the revised manual control system will be provided to NHTSA as a supplement to this report.

Toyota completed a vehicle inspection and field report for the incident on April 14, 2023. From the field report, Toyota obtained Vehicle Control History (VCH) and Event Data Recorder (EDR) data from the subject vehicle. VCH provides an approximately 8 second pre-crash recording, and EDR provides an approximately 5 second pre-crash recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed: The driver seat belt status was OFF (unbuckled) during the recording. Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged during the recording from approximately 6.35 seconds until approximately 3.6 seconds prior to the crash event, and again from approximately 2.35 to 1.15 seconds prior to the crash event. LTA was disengaged due to Lane Departure Alert (LDA) activation and sudden steering. At the time of LTA disengagement, the vehicle steering angle changed from 113 degrees (left) to approximately -95 degrees (right) before the collision with the highway divider. Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) was engaged from approximately 6.75 seconds until 0.35 seconds prior to the crash event. No FCW or AEB activation occurred.

Narrative:
The Ohmio Lift was driving on Gemende Drive towards Airport Drive in Riverside California. A minivan reversed out of a parking position (perpendicular parking to road lane) from the right side of the road into the shuttle¢ÂÂs path and struck the shuttle from the side.
After the incident a supervisor from the Riverside Transport Agency RTA (operator or the vehicle) was called to the side. The RTA supervisor recorded the incident according to RTAs protocols.
In addition to the Ohmio trainer/supervisor being on the vehicle additional Ohmio personal was called to the side as well.

Summary of Events:
-Upon detecting the minivan in the side envelope, the system issued a brake command within 5ms.
-Brake pressure began rising 58ms after the command and exceeded 90% of the requested pressure 164ms after the initial command.
-The minivan reversed out of a parking space perpendicular to the Ohmio LiftÃ¢ÂÂs direction of travel and struck the Lift on the side.
-The minivan continued reversing until contact occurred.
-The elapsed time from first detection of the minivan in the side envelope to impact was approximately 358ms.
-The vehicle came to a complete stop in 1.178 seconds.

In Summary:
The other car pushing out from the parking position did not give way as would have been required.
The Ohmio Lift detected the other car getting into the right side of its safety envelope just 358ms before the impact. The reaction time of the Ohmio Lift was as expected in terms of reacting to the signal and initiating a brake maneuver. However, the short time and distance between the other car entering the Ohmio Lift safety envelope (and consequently its track) was too short to avoid the collision. Even if the Ohmio Lift had come to a complete stop before the actual impact the collision would most likely have happened but potentially at a slightly different position.

As a result of the crash incident, multiple airbags deployed in the subject vehicle and it was towed away from the scene. According to the police report, at approximately 6:15 p.m. on July [XXX], 2024, the Nissan Ariya was traveling north on[XXX] in the number two lane when a tractor trailer traveling west bound on[XXX] attempted to make a left-hand turn onto [XXX] South, traveling across the northbound lane. According to the police report: the Ariya driver and passenger sustained fatal injuries and had to be extricated from the vehicle multiple airbags were deployed the passenger's seat belt use was "improper" the Ariya driver was belted and the tractor trailer driver was operating with a disqualified license.
Nissan obtained vehicle EDR from law enforcement. That data indicated that the speed at impact was 53.4 mph, with no pre-impact brake application. 
Nissan conducted a preliminary, non-destructive inspection on August [XXX], 2024. The vehicle had been stored in the open air and uncovered until August [XXX], 2024.  Various components were stored by the junkyard in an unidentified location and made available for inspection.  The vehicles condition is consistent with underride of the tractor trailer and extrication. 
The driver seatbelt was found buckled with the lap portion routed behind the seat, the pretensioner having activated and shoulder-belt webbing cut near the d-ring location. The passenger seatbelt was buckled, with both lap and shoulder belt pulled tight against the seat back, with the pretensioner having activated. 
Nissan was able to collect the vehicles ADAS control unit and Lane Camera assembly. Nissan was unable to download additional data from either system due to the nature of the incident which resulted in an immediate loss of supplied power to the assemblies, and consequently prevented event data from being stored in memory.
Nissan conducted an inspection of the trailer on October 9th. No findings during the inspection changed our understanding of the incident.
Nissan has identified no evidence that suggests that the incident was attributable to any defect or improper functioning of any of the vehicle's safety system.  Nissan has concluded its investigation into this incident.

Narrative:
Entries in this report are based on unconfirmed allegations:
On November 14, 2025, Toyota received initial contact from the mother, calling on behalf of her daughter. She alleged her daughter was involved in an accident where the cruise control on her 2024 Toyota Corolla got stuck and caused her to crash into a ditch. The caller believes there may have been a malfunction with the cruise control. As a result of the crash, the caller alleged that: the airbag deployed there were no serious injuries; and the vehicle was deemed a total loss by the insurance company. 

On January 9, 2026, Toyota completed a field report based on inspection of the subject vehicle. The field report contained EDR and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD) from the crash event. The PCS FFD showed that dynamic radar cruise control (DRCC) and lane trace assist (LTA) were engaged in the recorded moments leading to the crash event. Based on the engagement status of level 2 ADAS in moments leading up to the crash, this report is now being made. 

The EDR data and PCS FFD confirmed the driver did not apply the brakes until 1.5sec before the airbag deployment. After the brake switch became ON, cruise control and lane centering turned off appropriately, and deceleration was observed consistent with the brake application. The loss of control experienced by the driver and subsequent damage are likely caused by the road speed traveled (50mph in a 35mph speed zone approaching a T-intersection controlled by a stop sign at the intersection) and timing of brake application (1.5 sec before airbag deployment) prior to going through the intersection and off the road. Therefore, this will be the final update for this incident.

The customer provided a number for a case with the Georgia State Police: C001029793.

At 1:54 PM CDT on October 8, 2025 in Aledo, Texas, an Aurora truck traveling at approximately 7 mph on an I-20 frontage road in autonomy brushed against a temporary construction barrier. During development missions, Aurora tests new roads and conditions outside of its current ODD to prepare for safe driverless operations as Aurora expands its ODD. Two vehicle operators and a backseat rider were inside the vehicle.
While traversing a very narrow lane between temporary barriers and a ditch, slowly and with support of remote assist, the Aurora truck brushed a roadside barrier, resulting in minor scraping on the side of the truck. The Aurora vehicle operator then disengaged autonomy and manually drove the truck to Aurora's Fort Worth terminal.

No injuries were reported. No damage to the barrier was observed.

This incident occurred near Streetman, TX on [XXX] at approximately 3:03 PM CT on February [XXX], 2024. The Aurora vehicle was operating in autonomy at the time. Conditions were clear. As the Aurora vehicle was driving in its lane at 62 mph, a box truck veered into the lane of the Aurora vehicle. The box truck's mirror appeared to make contact with the back of the trailer that the Aurora Driver was pulling. At this time, we are not aware of any injuries, and camera footage appears to show that the box truck continued to drive. From the post-trip inspection, there was not any visible trailer damage. 
Before the collision, the Aurora Driver was driving straight in its lane and passing the box truck. Shortly thereafter, the box truck began to encroach into the lane of the Aurora Driver. The Aurora Driver detected the box truck's encroachment into the Aurora vehicle's lane and initiated a nudge away from the box truck to provide space. The Aurora Driver detected the collision and made the decision to initiate an incident response, but before it could execute that response, the Vehicle Operator took over control of the system and proceeded in manual. The Aurora vehicle then re-engaged in autonomy approximately two minutes later. 
The Vehicle Operator did not visually observe the collision, assumed the reaction of the Aurora Driver to be a software anomaly, and reported the vehicle nudge through our standard annotation protocol rather than through our incident response protocols. We identified the incident at approximately 1:03 PM CT on February [XXX], 2024 through a review of our data logs.

The driver originally alleged that the F-150 was at a complete stop and remained in that position for approximately 10 minutes before accelerating and colliding with a vehicle.  Ford Motor Company has now received notice through the driver's insurance company, that the driver claims that BlueCruise and One-Pedal driving were engaged at the time of the crash.  
BlueCruise can only be engaged and operate within designated BlueCruise Zones, and the location of the accident was more than 7 miles away from the nearest BlueCruise Operating Design Domain (ODD).  In addition, One-Pedal drive is unavailable when cruise control, adaptive cruise control, or adaptive cruise control with stop and go is active. Ford also conducted an EDR download, which indicates there was 100% accelerator pedal application and no brake application before impact. 
Ford has confirmed that the vehicle was equipped with ADAS Level 2 and BlueCruise. There are no reported injuries, and the insurer indicated it was closing the claim and accepting liability.  Ford now understands that the F-150 was towed from the scene after the crash.

A Ghost ADS-equipped car was driving engaged Northbound on [XXX]. As always, there were two safety drivers in the car. Traffic was moving in all four lanes at or near the speed limit. The Ghost vehicle was in the right-middle lane. Another vehicle (the "lead" car) entered into the Ghost car's lane from the right. While there were numerous vehicles ahead of the Ghost car before that vehicle entered the lane, the lead vehicle blocked the view of the lane before it. Throughout the incident, traffic in the other three lanes continued at a steady pace.
When the lead vehicle entered into the lane ahead of the Ghost car, the Ghost car applied the brakes to accommodate the intrusion and then continued to match the speed of the lead car. The lead car suddenly slammed the brakes. The Ghost car followed suit, reducing its speed from 19 mps (42.5 mph) to 4.7 mps (10.5 mph) within the next three seconds. The Ghost car was able to match the rapid speed reduction of the lead car and avoid contact.
The driver following the Ghost car was not able to respond as quickly as the Ghost ADS. When the following driver began to apply the brakes, the car was about five meters behind and was traveling at 6.5 mps. At the point of impact, the Ghost vehicle was traveling at 4.78 mps (10.7 mph), matching the lead car. There were no injuries. The vehicles suffered only cosmetic damage, the drivers exchanged information, and the Ghost safety drivers returned to home base in conventional mode.

Narrative: The May vehicle was involved in a rear-end collision shortly after completing a right-hand turn. As the vehicle proceeded through its turn, it encountered exhaust fumes from vehicles waiting at a stoplight in the adjacent lane. Due to environmental conditions and sensor limitations, the vehicle's lidar system interpreted the exhaust plume as a solid object in its path. In response, the autonomous vehicle first tried to adjust its position. When this maneuver proved insufficient, the system initiated a hard stop response. The vehicle behind, which was following at approximately 7-8 meters, was unable to stop in time and collided with the rear of the autonomous vehicle. The collision occurred at relatively low speeds (the autonomous vehicle had decelerated from approximately 7.6 m/s to 0 m/s), though exact impact speeds of the following vehicle were not recorded. The primary factor that led to this incident is that Lidar does not pierce through exhaust so the exhaust cloud appears to be a large, solid object. Some corrective actions that will be implemented: consider weather implication in future platform sensor selection and continue working on the software to improve a neural network to classify lidar points, which will use temporal information, radar, and camera features to make a decision on whether a lidar point is truly an object.

The report states that a disabled 2006 Toyota Prius was stopped in the left lane of traffic and that a 2012 Hyundai Elantra had stopped behind the Prius. The report further states that a 2022 Mach-E traveling in the left lane struck the Elantra from behind and that this initial collision pushed the Elantra forward, causing it to strike the Prius. The report states that the driver of the Hyundai and the driver of the Prius (who had exited the vehicle and was classified as a pedestrian) both sustained fatal injuries from the crash.
Based on further investigation, the following reflects Ford's understanding of the responsive facts and circumstances regarding this incident. On Sunday, March [XXX], 2024, about 3:20 a.m. eastern standard time, a 2022 Ford Mustang Mach-E electric-powered sport utility vehicle was traveling northbound in the left lane on [XXX] ([XXX]) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Mach-E was equipped with advanced driver assistance systems, including those providing partial automation capabilities that Ford refers to as "BlueCruise". Vehicle-based data obtained post-crash indicates that the vehicle's 23-year-old driver was using BlueCruise as it approached mile marker 26.8. At this location, [XXX] consisted of six traffic lanes, three each in the north- and southbound directions. The opposing lanes were divided by a concrete median barrier and the posted speed limit was 55 mph. some roadway lighting was present in this section of [XXX]. The Mach-E encountered two passenger vehicles that were stopped in the travel lanes of [XXX]. The Mach-E collided with the rear of the stationary 2012 Hyundai Elantra, which was attended by a 20-year-old driver. The Hyundai then collided with the rear of the stopped 2006 Toyota Prius, attended by a 21-year-old driver. At the time of the crash, the Hyundai driver was exiting the vehicle while the Toyota driver was standing near the front of the Hyundai. Narrative:
All of the data in this report and the following text is an excerpt from TuSimples original submission (30370-2949-1) and constitutes Navistars sole understanding of this event.
TuSimple's position is that this event does not meet the criteria for reporting under the SGO.
Specifically, the L4 ADS was not in operation at any point in the 30 seconds prior to making contact with the concrete barrier.
The event occurred as follows:
As the truck was being operated on the highway, within its mapped ODD, the driver and test engineer attempted to engage the ADS.
However, the ADS was not functional at that moment due to the computer unit not having been initialized, and should not have been
attempted to be activated. In short, this was a failed attempt to engage the system as a result of human error.
The system has now been modified to prevent the ADS from attempting to engage unless the health of the system is fully functional to
prevent human error from repeating this event.
When the erroneous attempt to engage occurred, the uninitialized vehicle control unit rotated the steering to the left, causing the truck to
veer left. The safety driver took control of the steering, and was able to steer accordingly, but not before the left front truck tire and left
front quarter panel came into contact with the concrete barrier to the left of the lanes of travel.

Customer requested that Kia repair the vehicle if not totaled by her insurance company.
The subject Kia Sportage is equipped with Highway Driving Assist (HDA).  HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving.  HDA may not be able to recognize all traffic situations and may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system.  Obstacles such as vehicles, motorcycles, bicycles, pedestrians, unspecified objects and structures that may collide with the vehicle may not be detected.
Based on the customer's comment of "by the time she realized it, I was not able to apply the brakes quick enough", it appears that the customer may have been distracted at the time of the incident. He indicated that he wanted, "someone at Lexus to explain how his vehicle's airbags did not deploy going 70mph on cruise control and lane assist." Additionally, the customer stated, "He and his friend that was in the passenger seat are slightly injured...he called 911 and they had a local tow service tow the vehicle to a lot." The customer stated that his driver seat belt was on, and that an occupant was in the rear seat laying down without the seat belt fastened. The customer also stated, "He and his friend that was in the passenger seat are slightly injured." and that, "knees are bothering the driver."
On Nov. 18, 2022, Toyota conducted further review of the customer's statement and determined that the crash was reportable.
On Nov. 30, 2022, Toyota received a field report related to the incident, which included Vehicle Control History (VCH) and Event Data Recording (EDR). VCH provides an approximately 7.7 second pre-crash recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.8 second pre-crash recording. From the data, Toyota observed that Lane Trace Assist (LTA) and Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) were engaged in the moments leading up to the crash event. LTA was engaged from the start of the recording until approximately 6.1 seconds prior to the crash event, at which point driver steering input disengaged the system. Prior to disengagement of LTA, the VCH recording shows the driver's hands were detected on the steering wheel.  DRCC was engaged from the start of the recording until the crash event. 
This report is a Monthly Update. The original report ID is 1306-4287-1.

Narrative:
On April [XXX], 2025, Toyota received a call from the subject vehicle owner stating that The caller was involved in a single-vehicle accident while driving their Toyota Prius on Highway [XXX] near Trinidad, California. It was raining heavily and the lane assist system nudged the vehicle, causing it to hydroplane and spin off the road. The vehicle sustained damage and was towed from the scene. The caller wanted to report the incident to Toyota in case it was an issue with the lane assist system that could affect other drivers. The caller also stated that the cruise control was not engaged at the time of the incident. Based on the customer statement that cruise control was not involved, this allegation was judged not SGO reportable at that time. Toyota initiated an inspection of the subject vehicle based on the customer allegations. 
On June 3, 2025, Toyota completed review of a field report of the investigation of the subject vehicle, which included EDR, Vehicle Control History (VCH) and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD). The VCH and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD) indicated that ADAS L2 was engaged in the recorded moments prior to the crash. The PCS FFD recording contains approximately 8 seconds of pre-crash data and images. From the PCS FFD, Toyota observed the following: Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) and Lane Trace Assist (LTA) were engaged from the start of the recording until 3.1 seconds prior to the collision. At this time, these systems were disabled when the brake switch turned on. The vehicle was traveling approximately 71mph leading up to the collision. The steering angle varied from -4.5 deg at the beginning of the recording to 48 deg at 1.8 sec prior to the crash, after which the images show the subject vehicle veering off the right side of the roadway.

*2/25/23: 1-Day Incident Report*
Customer contacted Kia Customer Care on 2/[XXX]/23 & reported that he was driving his 22 Kia Sorento 65mph on [XXX] near Meridian, CT when he fell asleep.  Customer stated he heard beeping, went to hit the brakes but it was too late & his vehicle rear ended the vehicle in front of him. The driver & passenger airbags deployed. The customer reported him & his wife were taken to the ER via ambulance. He reported that his upper body was sore (mostly wrist & left hand) & that his wife sustained a swollen ankle & bruising on the right side of her body. The vehicle was towed. Customer stated that he believed the accident was his fault but claims the Forward Collision Avoidance (FCA) system in this vehicle was not working properly. 
The subject 22 Sorento is equipped with Highway Driving Assist (HDA). HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance & speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway & helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. HDA may not be able to recognize all traffic situations. Obstacles such as vehicles, motorcycles, bicycles, pedestrians, unspecified objects & structures that may collide with the vehicle may not be detected. 
Based on the information currently available, Kia is unable to rule out that HDA was not engaged at the time of the incident. Kia is currently working on obtaining the ACU for further evaluation.
*3/6/23: 10-Day Update*
There are no new updates. Kia continues to work to obtain the ACU.
*3/15/23: Monthly Update*
Kia has requested & is waiting for the ACU from the customer's body shop.
*7/14/23: Monthly Update*
Kia received the ACU from the subject 2022MY Kia Sorento and downloaded the vehicle's EDR data.  The EDR data indicates that the incident did not occur during engagement of Level 2 ADAS.  The EDR data shows that the driver was applying the throttle via the accelerator pedal (44% throttle application). As a result, the driver was overriding the vehicle's ADAS functionality (i.e., Smart Cruise Control and Front Collision Avoidance) at the time of the incident.  Kia notes that the vehicle is designed with such override logic to give a driver's input priority over the ADAS features (e.g., perform emergency avoidance maneuvers, etc.)
In light of the above, Kia believes that this incident is no longer eligible for continued updates.

On December 4, 2025 at 7:30 PM PT a Waymo Autonomous Vehicle ("Waymo AV") operating in San Francisco, California was in a collision involving a motorcycle on Duboce Avenue near Elgin Park. 
The Waymo AV was stopped in-lane facing east on Duboce Avenue with its hazard lights activated for a passenger drop-off. While the Waymo AV was stopped, a motorcycle traveling eastbound on Duboce Avenue began passing the Waymo AV on the right, maneuvering between the Waymo AV and vehicles parked at the curb. As the motorcycle passed between the Waymo AV and the parked vehicles, a passenger inside the Waymo AV opened the rear right door and the motorcycle made contact with the open rear right door of the stationary Waymo AV. At the time of the impact, the Waymo AV's Level 4 ADS was engaged in autonomous mode. Both vehicles sustained damage. The passengers in the Waymo AV were not belted at the time of the collision as they were preparing to exit the Waymo AV.

Waymo is reporting this crash under Request No. 2 of Standing General Order 2021-01. Waymo may supplement or correct its reporting with additional information as it may become available.

The May vehicle was in autonomous mode on experimental test software (not deployed to the Commercial fleet), in light snow conditions.  A vehicle behind the AV was traveling approximately the same speed as the May shuttle. The May AV began to slow for an object ahead. Due to weather conditions, the AV misclassified a speed limit sign as a pedestrian, which intersected with the predicted trajectory of the AV. This caused the May AV to apply additional braking to avoid the projected collision with the misclassified object. The following vehicle did not react promptly when the May AV started to slow down, resulting in the following vehicle braking too late to avoid collision and impacting the May AV from behind.  The following vehicle then pulled around the May vehicle and drove away.  Resimulation of this event with an upcoming software version shows that the May AV would not misidentify the non-exist object so would not have decelerated unnecessarily. This improved software is set to be deployed to the full commercial fleet soon. In addition, per May policy, the commercial fleet would not operate in weather conditions like those present in this incident.

The customer alleged "his left shoulder hurt". The customer requested an inspection of the vehicle.
The subject Kia K4 is equipped with Lane Following Assist ("LFA"), Lane Keeping Assist ("LKA"), and Smart Cruise Control ("SCC"). It is unclear which feature the customer is referring to by "lane assist." However, only LFA and SCC engaged at the same could qualify as a Level 2 ADAS feature under the proper conditions.

LFA is a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road and assists the driver's steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. The functionality of LFA is contingent upon several outside factors and it is always the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle and to maintain the vehicle in its lane. 

Kia has attempted to contact the customer on several occasions to obtain additional information to evaluate the incident but customer has not responded.

** Monthly Update Report 12/15/2025***
KA received the subject vehicle's ACU and downloaded the vehicle's EDR data, which indicates that Smart Cruise Control was not engaged during the 5-seconds prior to the crash and thus vehicle was not being operated at LVL 2. The vehicle was steered rapidly to the left while being driven at highway speeds and then an evasive maneuver was performed steering the vehicle to the right. This amount of steering input exceeds what Lane Keep Asist / Lane Follow Asist can apply.  No Advanced Driving Assistance Systems that provide steering inputs were found to have been a contributing or causal factor in the collision. This information, including documents (subject vehicle EDR report, photos, customer care case, etc.) were provided to ODI engineer, Joseph Teitelman on 12/5/2025 per his request.

At approximately 5:54 p.m. on Wednesday, August [XXX], 2023, P84, travelling eastbound on [XXX], approached the three-way stop at [XXX] and [XXX]. P84 arrived at the intersection at the same time as two other vehicles: a grey van heading northbound on [XXX] and a red sedan heading westbound on [XXX]. The safety driver yielded to the northbound vehicle, which proceeded to make a right-hand turn eastbound onto [XXX]. After allowing the intersection to clear, the safety driver onboard P84 confirmed that it was safe for the shuttle to proceed through the intersection. As the shuttle entered the intersection, a second vehicle travelling northbound on [XXX], a white sedan, entered the intersection intending a left-hand turn onto westbound [XXX]. Both vehicles entered the intersection simultaneously, subsequently colliding at a low rate of speed in the middle of the intersection.  
At approximately 5:57 p.m., the Beep Command Center (BCC) was informed by the safety driver that P84 was involved in a minor collision with another vehicle at the intersection of [XXX] and [XXX]. The incident response protocol was initiated, and a supervisor dispatched to the scene. Local law enforcement (San Francisco Police Department) was contacted to report the collision but declined to respond given the minor nature of the collision, directing both parties to exchange information. After the Beep supervisor arrived on scene at approximately 6:49 p.m., the safety driver and supervisor removed the shuttle from the roadway and exchanged insurance information with the driver of the other vehicle. 
Damage to both vehicles was noted to be very minor. The shuttle sustained light scuffs, chips, and small paint transfer. The other vehicle sustained a small dent on the fender. Neither vehicle required towing, and both were safely driven from the scene. 
Beeps safety driver was subsequently subjected to a standard post-collision drug & alcohol screening which has since cleared.  
Contributing Factors 
Based on an analysis of the available evidence, Beep has determined the following factors may have contributed to the higher likelihood of a collision occurring in this instance: 
1.The white sedan failed to yield to P84 in accordance with California state law governing intersection priority.
2.The slight bend in P84s path to accommodate the lane shift through the intersection may have reduced the available stopping distance as the white sedan was not perceived as an obstacle in P84s path until it proceeded further into the intersection.
Incident Findings 
Beep developed the following findings regarding this incident:
1.P84 behaved as expected, detecting and maintaining awareness of the white sedan in the moments preceding the collision, commanding hard braking maneuver, and achieving a 3m/s2 deceleration rate once the white sedan encroached on P84s path.
2.The safety driver observed California state law and had the right of way when releasing P84 into the intersection.
3.The safety driver could have avoided the collision by using the emergency stop. The safety driver indicated that they were aware of the other vehicle through the duration of the incident and were aware of the proper procedure in this scenario but panicked in the moment.
Mitigation:
Implement a priority zone to account for the slight bend in the shuttles path and for future vehicles that may fail to yield.

Just before the next intersecting road [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]ell road [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] had sneezed and it often causes me to close my eyes.  The subject vehicle's side "headlamp area collided with a 2020 Dodge Durango striking them in the rear passenger area."  The owner alleges that a "warning light and sound activated, but the cars collision prevention system did not activate and stop the car before the impact was made," and that the airbags did not deploy. The subject Kia Niro is equipped with Highway Driving Assist (HDA), Lane Following Assist (LFA) and Smart Cruise Control (SCC). HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. HDA may not be able to recognize all traffc situations and may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system. LFA is also a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road, and assists the driver's steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. LFA does not operate at all times and it is the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle and to maintain the vehicle in its lane. 
 
It appears based on the owner's report that he was asleep at the time of the crash. Kia is working to inspect the vehicle, but has no further information at this time.

Update SGO Report 502-1470:
The son of the driver of the subject vehicle (who was not in the subject vehicle when the incident occurred) reported that the vehicle was being operated at 75-80mph in "self-driving mode" when the steering wheel locked, causing the driver to lose control of the vehicle and crash into an exit sign on the interstate. The driver's son reported that the vehicle then accelerated uncontrollably for 260 yards and crashed into a tree where it came to a stop. 
Additional investigation shows that the subject vehicle was traveling at 77mph with some form of cruise control engaged (either basic or adaptive cruise control) in the right lane of a six-lane, divided highway. The driver was unbelted, with a chime defeat device latched into the buckle of the driver's seatbelt. The lane in which the subject vehicle was traveling terminated at an exit ramp. Warnings that the lane was going to end were provided as early as 2000 feet (over 600 yards) in advance, and signs were posted cautioning drivers to reduce speed to 20mph on the exit ramp. For unknown reasons, the driver did not follow the lane onto the exit ramp and instead continued traveling straight off the road. Ford understands that the vehicle struck the exit sign and then continued off-road and struck a stump and then a tree.  
The driver of the subject vehicle was fatally injured in the crash.  
Ford records show that the subject vehicle was not equipped with the operating system necessary to make BlueCruise functional. The subject vehicle was equipped with both ACC and LCA. Ford has confirmed that the subject vehicle was being operated with some form of cruise control engaged when the incident occurred. Ford has not been able to confirm whether LCA was engaged at the time of (or within 30 seconds before) the accident.

Narrative:
The customer was traveling on a two lane, country road, which was missing lane markings on the sides of the road - only the middle line was properly marked. The speed limit on the country road is 35MPH. The customer noticed a pothole on the side of the road, swerved towards the middle of the road to avoid it, but the LKA assist engaged and moved the vehicle back in the lane. By doing so, the vehicle ran over the pothole, with both front and back passenger side tires and damaged both wheel and tires in the process. During our investigation, we determined that in this case the LKA worked as intended. The system is designed to prioritize a solid line, and can't detect a pothole, and since the road is very narrow (our estimate is less than 3m per side) the vehicle unfortunately ran over the pothole. LKA/ELK system limitations throughout the industry are similar: the LKA/ELK systems try to keep vehicle inside the lane, to prevent a vehicle from drifting out, and the system can't predict driver intention, for example: Is the driver crossing solid lane intentionally or by accident, is hard to distinguish. Relevant override conditions in this case are:
- Steering wheel speed  200deg/s
- Steering torque  3.5Nm
In our application, the override force is limited by the EU homologation test and therefore, we feel that the vehicle behaved as expected and should have been over-powered by the driver to avoid the pothole, thus eliminating a costly replacement cost of two wheels and tires.

The accelerator pedal was at 0%, with the Dynamic Radar Cruise Control on and the vehicle travelling at a sustained 63.4 MPH. The steering angle was constant at 1.5 degrees until the impact event. Some entries in this report are based on unconfirmed allegations. On January 18, 2023 Toyota completed a field report related to this crash incident, in which the owner's allegation was related to Pre-Collision System (PCS) non-activation. The owner alleged she was driving on [XXX] through the [XXX], "when another vehicle entered the intersection to her left, driving at a high rate of speed." She also claimed that she, "had a green light, and the other vehicle ran a red light," and she, "struck the other vehicle in its right side with the front of her Lexus." After the initial impact, the owner's vehicle "spun to the right, then came to a stop." The owner alleged that her, "vehicle's Pre-Collision System should have stopped the car and avoided the accident," and the, "PCS system did not function."
There were no allegations made related to the operation of Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) or Lane Trace Assist (LTA). However, upon obtaining and reviewing VCH and EDR data from the crash event, Toyota became aware that the vehicle was operating with ADAS L2 engagement in the moments leading up to the crash event. VCH provides an approximately 7.9 second pre-crash data recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.8 second pre-crash data recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed: LTA was engaged from the start of the recording until approximately 1 second prior to the crash event. DRCC was engaged from the start of the recording until the crash event. The PCS warning (FCW) and  Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) did not activate during the recording of the event, because the Lexus Safety System generation of this vehicle (LSS + 2.0) does not support cross traffic PCS functions. 
As a result of the crash event, multiple airbags deployed in the owner's vehicle which was towed from the scene. The owner claimed that she, "could not breathe because of the accident. She said her left wrist was bruised, her left knee is sore and her ribcage hurts."

Guest states her son was in the emergency room for 6-7 hours and then released."
On August 8, 2024, Toyota completed review of a field report of the investigation of the subject vehicle. which included EDR, Vehicle Control History (VCH) and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD). The VCH and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD) indicating that ADAS L2 was engaged in the recorded moments prior to the crash. The PCS FFD recording contains approximately 8 seconds of pre-crash data and images. From the PCS FFD, Toyota observed the following: Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) was engaged from the start of the recording until the time of the collision. Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged from the start of the recording until approximately 4.8 seconds prior to the collision, and was suspended due to driver steering (EOS torque) over LTA threshold. The vehicle was traveling approximately 78mph leading up to the collision. The steering angle input was steady at -4.5 deg from the beginning of the recording until 0.4 seconds prior to the collision, after which the images show the subject vehicle veering into the lane of the heavy truck, with the steering angle increasing to 31.5 deg at the trigger event. The driver applied the brakes 1.6 seconds after the collision.

On January [XXX], 2023, RRAI received a support request through their Customer Support Portal from Beep, Inc., the owner of the vehicle, regarding their Olli 2.0 vehicle bumping into the curb in Peachtree Corners, GA. No one was injured and the only damage was to the vehicle itself. The customer contacted RRAI through the client support portal shortly after the incident. No injuries occurred, there were no passengers besides the safety operator, no other vehicles were involved, and no emergency systems were engaged.
Olli 2.0 (S/N 2-18) is an 8-passenger shuttle that is no longer manufactured. The vehicle manufacturer, Local Motors, dissolved in 2022. Local Motors contracted RRAI to install autonomy kits for several Olli shuttles during the period of 2018 - 2020. RRAI provided some support for initial site deployment and ensured customer safety operators were trained on the autonomy system. Since the Local Motors dissolution in 2022, almost all Olli vehicles have been decommissioned.
To date, we have concluded the following:
1. There were no updates or alterations made by RRAI in the months prior to Jan [XXX]. In previous operations, including the immediately preceding operations on January 20th, 2023, Olli 2-18 ran the route as normal with no anomalies. There were no software updates or other system changes before it was run again on January [XXX], 2023, the date of curb contact.
2. The root cause of the curb contact was a communication error with the HD Map registration module. HD Map registration utilizes real-time lidar and positioning data and compares that to a-priori HD maps stored within the autonomy system. A communication problem occurred between the computer running the map registration software and the computer running the navigation algorithms. The cause for the communication problem has been identified and a fix has been implemented to prevent the issue from happening again (see below).
3. Steering was out of calibration. It was noted through data collection that the steering was out of calibration at time of incident. The autonomy system was attempting to correct this issue, but the vehicular steering system could not achieve the required turn radius. This is a vehicular maintenance concern managed by the customer.
It was determined that the HD map registration issue had not been observed during autonomous operations in the previous four years. The solution to prevent further occurrences includes:
1. Implementing a self-diagnostic routine upon system boot, which ensures the communication connection is established. If the connection is not established, this diagnostic will prevent the vehicle from driving autonomously. 
2. Updating the error checks to ensure that during run time, the vehicle will come to a controlled stop in event of a communication problem.  
3. Working with the customer to recalibrate the steering, and assisting in reviewing customer's vehicle maintenance checks for steering calibration if necessary.
4. Continuing to review data to determine other concerns or improvements.

On December 11, 2025, Ford received notification of an incident, involving an 2025 F-150.  The incident occurred on December 8, 2025. Customer further alleged the vehicle drifted 2 lanes to the left and made impact with the center road barrier resulting in the deployment of the airbag and non-specified injuries. Customer further alleges that the HDA (Highway Driving Assist) may not have been functioning properly. Customer did not contact Kia regarding the incident. The vehicle was instead located  a Copart facility. Kia Customer Care is in the process of reaching out to the insurance company to obtain permission to inspect the vehicle. *11/9/22 10-Day Update*
Kia is tentatively scheduled to inspect the subject vehicle located  Copart in San Martin, CA on 11/17/22. At that time, Kia will also download/read available EDR data. As a result, Kia has no additional information at this time and has not received any contact from the customer.
*12/15/22 Monthly Update*
Kia NASO Engineers inspected the subject EV6 vehicle (VOQ 11491182) on 11/17/22  Copart in San Martin, CA. Based on the inspection and the EDR report, no faults were found with any of the vehicle's systems and appears to be lack of driver control as mentioned by the driver in the VOQ. And per Matthew Yandrick of ODI's request, a copy of the EDR report was provided to NHTSA via the secure link-SLFTS under confidentially on 11/30/22.
*1/17/23 Monthly Update*
On 1/4/23, Kia received an email from ODI Electronics Engineer, Matthew Yandrick, requesting additional information regarding this incident.  Below are the 3 questions from Matthew and Kia's responses which were provided to Matthew on 1/11/23:
1) Was the steering angle parameter recorded? The EDR shows a steering input parameter.
Kia response: Yes, steering angle parameter is recorded and is identified on the report as being 0 degrees which represents a steering wheel pointed approximately straight ahead and is not a null value. Note that the steering angle is reported in increments of 5 degrees in the EDR of this vehicle.
2) The consumer alleges Lane Keep Assist was engaged. Has Kia been able to confirm this?
Kia response: No. There is no data in the EDR of this vehicle regarding any Lane Safety function status, and we have not been able to confirm if it was engaged at the time of the crash. Also, due to front end damage causing system errors, engineers were unable to access the driver-selectable settings for LKA to determine the function status (Off, Warning Only, or Active Assist).
3) The consumer alleges the incident occurred on a multi-lane road with a center barrier. Can Kia confirm the location of the incident? 
Kia response: This was an incident initiated from a VOQ and not by a communication from the consumer to Kia and thus Kia did not receive the location information. However, per your request, Kia has attempted to reach out to the consumer to see if such information is available and awaiting response.
*2/15/23 Monthly Update*
On 1/19/23, customer contact achieved. Engineer determined customer may not have understood limitations of HDA and LFA disablement when driver hands off wheel.

VCH provides an approximately 7 second pre-crash data recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.7 second pre-crash data recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed: LTA was engaged during the recording from approximately 6 seconds until approximately 3 seconds prior to the crash event, at which point the driver's steering input disengaged the system. At the time of LTA disengagement, the driver turned the vehicle right at a steering angle increasing from 53 degrees to 465 degrees. DRCC was engaged during the recording until approx. 1.7 seconds prior to the crash event. No FCW or AEB activation occurred.
As a result of the crash incident, no airbags deployed in the subject vehicle and it was towed from the crash scene.
This report is a 10-Day update. The original report ID is 1306-5139-1.

Based on the facts currently available, there is no indication that the HDA system was not working properly.  Kia is submitting this report as a precautionary measure because the customer reported HDA was engaged at the time of the incident and and it appeared to meet the other requirements under the SGO.

Narrative: The May Mobility vehicle (Ego) approaches a turn with a trailing vehicle following closely behind. The May planner initially selects a trajectory it believes will safely complete the turn. However, as the Ego begins the turn, it re-evaluates the situation and detects a significant risk of striking the curb. At that point, the planner shifts focus from avoiding the curb entirely to minimizing the severity of a potential curb strike. To reduce speed before the expected contact, the Ego brakes at 3.5 m/sÂ²). Because the trailing vehicle is following so closely, this deceleration makes a rear-end collision likely. The Ego predicts a potential rear-end collision and elects to reduce brake force to lessen the impact severity. Moments later, the trailing vehicle strikes the rear driver-side bumper of the Ego and then drives away. Future improvements are underway to give the planner a policy option to steer away from curbs. This new capability will help the vehicle avoid situations where braking becomes the only remaining way to manage close curb proximity.

Toyota received an allegation related to this crash on April 11, 2023, and later on April 14, 2023 from the owner and driver of the vehicle through a call to the Toyota Brand Engagement Center. The contact record indicates that the owner alleged he was driving on [XXX] when the vehicle, "veered off the road somehow and crashed into a field." The owner's primary allegation was related to the airbags not deploying. He also mentioned being, "uncomfortable with the steering corrections and with lane departure." The owner described his injuries as a concussion and a partially collapsed lung. Additionally, the owner stated that the White City Police Department responded to the incident and created Police Report # SP23096093. On April 28, 2023, Toyota completed a vehicle inspection and field report for the incident. There were no allegations made related to the Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) or Lane Trace Assist (LTA). However, on May 2, 2023, after additional analysis of the recorded vehicle data, Toyota determined the case was reportable under the SGO. 
Toyota obtained Vehicle Control History (VCH) and Event Data Recorder (EDR) data from the subject vehicle. VCH provides an approximately 7 second pre-crash recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.7 second pre-crash data recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed: The driver seat belt status was OFF (unbuckled) during the recording. LTA was engaged during the recording from approximately 4 seconds until approximately 1.6 seconds prior to the crash event. At the time of LTA disengagement, the driver turned the vehicle left at a steering angle increasing from approximately 4.5 degrees to 88.5 degrees. DRCC was engaged during the recording until approximately 0.8 seconds prior to the crash event. No FCW or AEB activation occurred. 
As a result of the crash incident, the subject vehicle's curtain shield airbags deployed, the front seatbelt pretensioners deployed and were locked in the retracted position, and it was towed from the crash scene. The front driver and passenger airbags did not deploy.
This report is a 10-Day update. The original Report ID is 1306-5424-1.

The subject vehicle was travelling northbound on [XXX] at a stated speed of 45 MPH with Adaptive Cruise Control(ACC) and Lane Centering (LCF) engaged. The customer stated that she had been driving for 10 hours and that it was raining heavily, with low visibility. The vehicle left the roadway at a rail crossing and came to rest parallel with the railroad tracks with the RH side of the vehicle centered within the tracks. The impact with the tracks deflated all four tires and caused damage to the right front bumper cover. There was also damage reported to certain suspension and steering components and the vehicle undercarriage. There were no airbags deployed and the vehicle was towed from the scene. The customer reported minor injuries and was not provided, nor sought immediate medical attention. During a follow-up conversation, the customer indicated that she came upon a road that turned left and,  because of the heavy rain she did not see the curve.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on 3/12/2024. Prior to the inspection, the customer provided a diagram of the scene, indicating that the vehicle had actually been travelling in an east-bound direction and that it was a right-hand turn, not left-hand as originally stated. A site visit indicated that the roadway was a country lane with no lane markings. The curve was a sharp (90-degree) turn to the right signposted with an arrow identifying the direction in which to turn. Though there were no previous signs to indicate the approaching turn, there was a Truck Crossing (W11-10) sign 0.3 miles before the turn to alert motorists in advance of locations where unexpected entries into the roadway, which included a recommended speed of 25 MPH.
[REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]
Based on the inspection, the data acquired and the customer's narrative, Subaru determined that the customer was likely using the ACC, but not LCF, on a roadway with no markings, during a period of heavy rain and low visibility, at a speed that exceeded the posted and recommended speed limits. The customer failed to notice the approaching sharp turn to the right and did not apply the brakes in time to appropriately slow the vehicle to a speed that would allow it to safely navigate the turn. As a result, the customer lost control of the vehicle, which left the roadway and came to rest on the railroad tracks.

9/13/2024 Update to 855-8237-2:
MBUSA conducted a scene and vehicle inspection on August 14, 2024, which included a physical examination of the vehicle. The subject vehicle was located in a salvage yard. The subject vehicle was left uncovered, exposing the vehicle to rain and other weather conditions (including heavy rains associated with Tropical Storm Debby). A significant amount of standing water was observed in both the driver and passenger footwells. As a result of this water damage to the subject vehicle, MBUSA was not able to establish a connection to the vehicle system diagnostics, control units, or EDR. 
A physical inspection of the braking and steering systems was subsequently performed. This inspection did not identify evidence of any steering or braking malfunction and the available information indicates both systems operated as intended at the time of the incident. The dashcam videos provided by the owner show the driver increasing the vehicles speed from 35mph at the start of the video to 46.5mph at the time of the crash. No audible warnings or steering wheel movement were observed in the driver-facing video. When DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist is active, the vehicle is designed to allow a driver to overrule and suppress the system by depressing the accelerator pedal. Based on the speed increase observed in the provided videos, it suggests that the system was not providing speed control to the subject vehicle prior to the incident.
Based on its investigation and review of the videos provided by the vehicle owner, MBUSA has concluded that that the vehicle operated as intended and that DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist was likely not engaged during the 24-second period captured by the dashcam video recording and when the driver lost consciousness. MBUSA has concluded its investigation into this matter.

Customer contacted Kia's Customer Care Center on 1/4/24 to provide details regarding an incident that had occurred on 12/14/23 involving his 2023MY Kia Telluride. Customer reported that while driving, along w/ 3 passengers, on [XXX] in the State of GA, there was a bend in the road & the vehicle didn't make the turn in time & the vehicle ran into wet grass. The customer stated he was unable to recover control of the vehicle once it made contact w/ the wet grass. Customer reported that the vehicle "hit berms, trees, signs & also began to roll until the vehicle settled to a stop." The customer reported he was driving 77mph in a 70mph zone. The customer indicated that Highway Driving Assist (HDA) and Smart Cruise Control (SCC) features were engaged 30 seconds before the incident. The airbags deployed & reported minor injuries of "cuts, scratches, wounds, bumps & bruises". The customer alleged that the lane departure system didn't work properly & wanted a new vehicle or compensation in order to purchase another vehicle. Kia notes that based on available information, the incident occurred in FL.
The subject Kia Telluride is equipped w/ HDA, Lane Following Assist (LFA) and SCC. HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance & speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway & helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. HDA may not be able to recognize all traffic situations & may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system. LFA is also a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road, & assists the driver's steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. LFA does not operate at all times & it's the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle & to maintain the vehicle in its lane. Based on the available information, the customer appears to have a misunderstanding of the capabilities of the vehicle's LFA function & appears to have relied on LFA to steer the vehicle.
*1/16/24: Monthly Update
Kia is working w/ ODI engineer, Joe Teitelman to schedule a joint inspection of the subject vehicle in Jacksonville, FL. The owner has consented to the EDR being downloaded which will be done when the vehicle is inspected. At the time of this update, the current proposed date for inspection is set for 1/31/24. Kia has no further information at this time.
*2/15/24: Monthly Update
The joint inspection with ODI engineer Joseph Teitelman occurred on 1/31/24. On 2/12/24, Kia submitted the EDR report w/ a request for confidentiality via NHTSA's SLFTS portal. On 2/14/24, Joseph Teitelman also requested the diagnostic reports from the subject vehicle which was submitted by Kia w/ a CBI request the following day, 2/15/24 via NHTSA SLFTS portal.
*3/15/24: Monthly Update
Kia engineer reviewed the EDR data previously submitted to NHTSA and identified the following: 1) the vehicle's safety restraint systems operated normally & without fault in each impact 2) the SCC system was engaged before the crash, however, the throttle was being pressed by the driver, overriding the system's operation and 3) the EDR does not record any lane assist function operation, however, the steering angles recorded in the data from -3.0 to 0.0 seconds before crash are above the threshold for what the system can provide both for rate of rotation and total angle. As a result, no vehicle or manufacturing concern was identified and the cause of the crash was most likely due to driver error.

Narrative:
Customer contacted Kia via Web Note on June 24, 2025, and reported he was involved in an accident while driving his 2024MY Kia Sportage with "Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) enabled at approximately 40-45MPH." Customer claimed that another vehicle was stopped at a traffic light and the subject vehicle "did not slow down as expected." Customer then "attempted to disengage the ACC and manually apply the brakes," but "the system failed to respond, preventing me from stopping the vehicle." Customer added that "the ACC system did not reduce speed appropriately or allow me to take manual control in [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] to avoid the crash." Customer reported there was a "significant collision", during which the airbags deployed. He confirmed that he was able to drive the vehicle away from the scene.
Customer reported sustaining injuries to his thumb and stomach "because of [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] seat belt" and requested warranty coverage, a vehicle replacement, and compensation. The customer confirmed they were not transported to the hospital and is not currently under any medical attention.
Kia Customer Care ("CC") contacted customer to obtain additional information regarding the incident. Customer reported that Highway Driving Assist (HDA), Smart Cruise Control (SCC) and Lane Following Assist (LFA) were also on at the time of the incident and provided post-incident photos of the vehicle. The photos provided by the customer show damage to the center portion of the front bumper, consistent with contact against the rear tow hitch on the other vehicle which is also visible in the photos. Kia escalated the case for further review.
Kia confirmed that both SCC and LFA were engaged at the time of the crash. While the customer reported that HDA was also active, Kia confirmed that HDA was not engaged at the time of the crash. Kia also reviewed the ECU data which confirmed that the brake pedal was pressed two seconds before impact, which disengaged the SCC system. The data also indicates that the Forward Collision-Avoidance Assist ("FCA") system detected a vehicle ahead and issued a Level 1 audible and visual warning prior to the collision. These data points suggest that the driver did not brake early or forcefully enough to avoid the collision.
The subject Kia Sportage is equipped with HDA, LFA, and Smart Cruise Control (SCC). Another name for SCC is Adaptive Cruise Control, which is how the customer refers to the system. LFA is a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road and assists the driver's steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. The functionality of LFA is contingent upon several outside factors and it is always the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle and to maintain the vehicle in its lane.
Further, post-impact drive cycle data shows no braking concerns. The vehicle was driven away from the scene without reported braking issues, and the brake system continued to function as expected.
Kia is currently working to obtain additional information to evaluate this incident.
*** 8/15/2025 Monthly Update ***
On July 15, 2025, Kia received a request from Mr. Teitelman via email for materials relating to the incident report. On July 23, 2025, Kia provided Mr. Teitelman the requested information via NHTSA's SLFTS portal. In addition, the customer has since stated he is unable to provide any additional information because he sold the vehicle to his insurance provider. Kia has no further information.

Additional verbatim text of follow-up inquiry by Mazda Customer Experience Center representative to customer is provided:
"The customer stated that he was in the right lane and he wanted to merge into the left lane customer stated as he turned his head for a min to check before merging over the car in front of him stopped really fast and his car just reveled up to 20 mphs for no reason he stated that the car just took off and hit the car in front of him he stated that he didn't hit the gas or anything he stated everything happened so fast that he couldn't even hit his breaks to try to stop the car. ( The 1st time the customer was telling me what happened he stated that the car that was in front of him was at a complete stop and his car just took off for no reason the customer also stated that when he got on the highway about 10-15 minutes of driving, he had turned the system on and set if for 20 mph but nothing happened he stated then while driving the car did a couple jumps then took off and hit the car in front of him"
Points of clarification/interpretation in order to explain the details of this incident are provided:
"Traffic Jam" Mode was used to describe Mazda's Traffic Jam Assist (TJA) ADAS-2 function, which is alleged to have been operating for some time prior to the crash.
The driver indicated the TJA function was active while driving on the highway, at some point the driver disengaged the TJA function by applying brakes for unknown reasons, followed by reactivating TJA at a later point.
Eventually the reported crash occurred.
No injuries were reported as a result of the incident.
No air bags were deployed as a result of the incident.
The subject vehicle was towed away from the incident scene.
(July 10, 2023 update)
On June 23 2023, Mazda opened an investigation to verify Connected Vehicle (CV) data.   On July 2 2023, Mazda confirmed from CV data analysis that the level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS), known as Traffic Jam Assist (TJA), was cancelled by pressing the brake pedal thirty-nine seconds prior to collision.   For this reason, it was concluded that the TJA system had no influence on causing the crash incident to occur.   
As this vehicle was verified to disengage the level 2 ADAS system more than thirty seconds prior to collision, this case does not meet reporting criteria under the Second Amended Standing General Order 2021-01.  Mazda considers this incident closed with no further reporting obligations.

On September [XXX], 2022, a Kia Customer Care Center (CC) agent was dispatched a case where the customer is alleging the "collision assistance feature did not follow through" resulting in a rear end collision with a 2022 Ford Expedition.  Customer alleges he was traveling approximately 50mph on [XXX] with a following distance of 60-80ft with various safety features active including lane keeping assist, Forward Collision Avoidance and adaptive cruise control.  The customer stated the Expedition had a broken taillight and it was difficult to determine whether the vehicle was slowing down.  Customer noticed his Kia EV6 was not slowing down as his vehicle was approaching the Expedition at approximately 40ft causing him to manually pressed on the brakes.  Customer reported that after depressing the brakes, the collision avoidance alarm sounded but the brakes felt "spongy".  Customer alleges the system did not apply what the customer believed to be maximum braking power, even though he had the brakes fully depressed.  Customer rear-ended the Expedition at 15mph. The customer's vehicle was towed.  When asked by CC, the customer reported that HDA and cruise control were engaged at the time of the incident but the customer did not allege that either of those systems caused the accident. 
The subject Kia EV6 is equipped with the ADAS Level 2 Highway Driving Assist (HDA).  HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between the lanes while driving.  However, there is no indication from the facts currently available that the HDA system was not working properly.  Kia is currently working on scheduling an inspection of the vehicle.
**9/[XXX]/2022 10-Day Update**
Kia inspected the subject 2022 EV6 vehicle on September [XXX], 2022 and downloaded the vehicles EDR data. Based upon a review of the data, the subject vehicle did not have Smart Cruise Control with Stop & Go (SCC w/ Stop & Go) engaged at least in the last 5 seconds prior to the crash.  In order for HDA to operate, SCC must be engaged.  The EDR data identifies the following:  1) Sign of the last accelerator input is 2.5 seconds prior to crash 2) the first sign of brake pedal input is at 1 second prior to crash 3) the vehicles FCA (Frontal Crash Avoidance) system started warning the driver from 1.6 seconds prior to crash all the way to point of crash and went through all 3 levels of FCA warning (Level 1 warning 1.6-1.4 seconds before crash, Level 2 warning 1.3-0.6 seconds before crash, and the last Level 3 0.5 seconds to point of crash.).
Based on the EDR data, the accident was not caused by a failure and/or disengagement of HDA.

On December 13, 2022 Toyota received a field report related to this crash incident, in which the owner's allegation was related to airbag non-deployment. During the crash event, the vehicle was rear-ended by an SUV, then crashed into the back of a passenger car. There were no allegations made related to the operation of the ADAS systems. However, upon obtaining and reviewing VCH and EDR data from the crash event, Toyota became aware that the vehicle was operating with ADAS L2 engagement in the moments leading up to the crash event. VCH provides an approximately 9 second pre-crash data recording, and EDR provides an approximately 4.8 second pre-crash data recording. Based on the data obtained, the following information was observed: Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged during the recording until approximately 4 seconds prior to the crash event. Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) was engaged during the recording until approximately 2.4 seconds prior to the crash event, at which point the PCS Alarm (FCW) was activated. The vehicle was traveling at approximately 70 MPH prior to applying the brakes. As a result of the crash incident, the vehicle was towed away from the scene. The owner alleged the vehicle's driver was experiencing, "back pain and headaches."
This report is a 10-Day update. The original report ID is 1306-4427-1.

Entries in this report are based on unconfirmed allegations.
On August 9, 2023, Toyota received an allegation related to this crash from the vehicle owner and mother of the driver who was operating the vehicle during the crash event. On August 10, 2023, through additional contact with the driver of the vehicle, Toyota was notified that the crash resulted in the vehicle being towed from the scene. 
The contact record indicates that driver alleged the following: the driver alleged that, "the lane assist malfunctioned while cruise control was on." The driver stated he was driving on [XXX] (direction unknown) with the "adaptive cruise control and lane assist turned on". He stated that he, "had two hands on the wheel and had a secure grip, when he saw a light on the dashboard for the lane assist and the vehicle just veered to the left." He, "attempted to correct the direction but ended up fishtailing and losing control, ultimately hitting a cable barrier that was on the left" He stated that the cable barrier protected him from going into oncoming traffic, but it damaged the entire left side and front of the vehicle. He also stated that none of the airbags deployed and he was not injured. The police responded, and he had the car towed from the scene to a body shop.
On September 11, 2023 Toyota completed a field report for a vehicle inspection related to the incident, and EDR, Vehicle Control History (VCH), and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD) were recovered from the vehicle. The PCS FFD has an approximately 8 second pre-crash data recording. From  the PCS FFD, Toyota observed that Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged until approximately 8 seconds before the crash event, and Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) was engaged until approximately 2 seconds before the crash event. The LTA (ADAS L2) disengagement was due to lack of driver input. Specifically, the TSS system detected no "driver steering wheel hold" for a certain amount of time, and suspended the operation after multiple driver visual and audible alerts. After the LTA suspension, at approximately 3 seconds prior to the crash event, the driver steered the vehicle left at approximately 27 degrees, veering off the road.  The Vehicle Stability Control System activated at approximately 2.5 seconds prior to the crash event, which disengaged DRCC. 
The police report from the Calhoun County Sheriff's department is 23003098.
